extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and activists interested in media ownership and media policy
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and normative criteria for assessing the effects of corporate concentration in news/media and what broadcasting should provide in the public interest. Focuses on ownership, diversity, access, and democratic information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of news, opinion, and commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: The public interest is to have the country's largest broadcasting system ... provide diversity in news, opinion, and commentary that serves all Americans, right, left, and independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters should offer a range of perspectives across the political spectrum so that all segments of the public can access differing viewpoints. Diversity is named as central to serving the public interest and to protecting democratic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to local stations (localism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide access to their local stations as well as true choices in national programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media policy should ensure local communities retain access to local broadcasters and local content; concentration should not erode localism or local control of programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: True choices in national programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast systems should provide 'true choices in national programs' rather than narrowing available national political/cultural options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National programming ought to offer meaningful alternatives rather than homogenized, cartel-driven content that limits voters' exposure to options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of democratic information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: A country without all the significant news, points of view, and information its citizens need to be informed voters is risking the loss of democratic rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media should supply the 'significant news' and information necessary for voters to make informed decisions; failing this standard is presented as threatening democracy itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public stewardship of the airwaves
rubrics_metrics.description: The public owns the air waves, not the broadcasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast spectrum is a public resource and licensees have obligations to serve public interests; this underpins arguments for regulation, ownership limits, and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on ownership concentration / antitrust enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Media Monopoly describes the cartel of five giant media conglomerates ... their power has led to the government's somnolence of anti-trust action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantive standard is that ownership concentration should be checked by active antitrust enforcement; failure to act permits cartel-like behavior that harms diversity and democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of ownership and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The book describes these dominant media giants, how they cooperate with each other in the manner of a cartel, who runs them, and how this all came to pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider who controls media organizations and their cooperative relationships; transparency about ownership and corporate ties is necessary to understand influence on content and politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural responsibility (avoid manufacturing degrading values)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media conglomerates ... have almost single-handedly as a group, in their radio and television dominance, produced a coarse and vulgar culture that celebrates the most demeaning characteristics in the human psyche: greed, deceit, and cheating as a legitimate way to win (as in the various 'reality' shows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media ought not to promote demeaning or corrosive social values; cultural impact (e.g., promotion of greed or deceit) is a criterion when assessing media practices and programming choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: These five huge corporations ... are unique among all huge corporations: they are a major factor in changing the politics of the United States and they condition the social values of children and adults alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should measure how media ownership affects political discourse and policy, including whether conglomerates actively shape political orientations (e.g., driving conservative or far-right politics).
